result: Testing the LGR clonal marking system with four 1-hour heat shocks over 3 days revealed all six expected marker combinations with progressive decrease in clonal diversity, but less overall diversity than reported by Reilein et al., with never more than four uniquely marked clones per ovariole compared to up to six in the prior study.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 provide consistent experimental observations using the LGR system with quantitative data (n>300 ovarioles) showing reproducible patterns but systematic differences from Reilein et al. The data are internally consistent and supported by Figure 1A-E.

result: In ovarioles with more than two distinctly labeled lineages using the LGR system, 88.7% had only 1-2 lineages spanning the entire ovariole while other lineages were small, suggesting predominance of one or two FSC lineages. Multiple heat shocks may produce subclones, and single heat shock reduced the number of distinctly labeled clones.
evaluation: Claims C52-C58 present quantitative observations (88.7%, n=62) with appropriate controls (single vs. multiple heat shocks) and logical interpretation about subclone generation. The data support the inference that apparent clonal diversity may be artifactual, though alternative explanations remain possible.

result: The LGR clonal marking system showed high background clone induction (47% total: 25% FSC clones, 22% transient clones) without heat shock, compared to <2% for the GFP negative system and 2% reported by Reilein et al., indicating the LGR system lacks robust low background clone induction.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide direct quantitative comparison between systems (n=188 for GFP negative, n=112 for LGR) with appropriate controls. The large discrepancy (47% vs 2%) is well-documented and reproducibility issues are appropriately noted. Data shown in Figure 2A-B.

result: The LGR system produced clones with unexpected marker combinations (LacZ-, GFP-, RFP+ and LacZ-, GFP-, RFP-) that are not predicted by the genotype, occurring in both heat-shocked and non-heat-shocked cohorts with healthy, dividing cells, revealing significant flaws that severely reduce the system's reliability for determining FSC number.
evaluation: Claims C63-C73 document unexpected marker patterns with appropriate controls (internal positive controls, cell morphology analysis, mitotic state assessment). The genetic logic in C65 is sound, and multiple alternative explanations are ruled out systematically. The conclusion about system unreliability (C71-C73) follows logically from the data shown in Figure 2C-E.

result: The assumption in Reilein et al. that FRT recombination occurs at both sites in 100% of mitotic cells is challenged by observed marker frequencies showing unrecombined phenotype (LacZ+, GFP+, RFP+) as most common, unequal fitness of cells lacking different markers, and prior literature showing incomplete recombination even with constitutive Flp expression.
evaluation: Claims C74-C86 provide strong critique of a key assumption in Reilein et al. through empirical data (Figure 3A), established knowledge about FRT systems (C77-C80), and the authors' own experience (C81). The quantitative marker frequency data directly contradict the 1:1:1:2:2:2 ratio assumed in the prior study.

result: Using the FRT19A GFP negative system, 94% of ovarioles with clones showed contiguous FSC clone patterns (61.5% large FSC clones, 20.6% transient clones, 3.6% FSC replacement pattern), with only 6% showing discontinuous patterns, confirming that FSC clones typically form coherent, contiguous units contributing to every follicle.
evaluation: Claims C87-C96 provide comprehensive quantitative classification of clone patterns (n=136) with clear categories and percentages. The data directly address the discontinuous clone hypothesis from Reilein et al. and are supported by Figure 3B-G. The conclusion is appropriately qualified regarding rare discontinuous patterns.

result: Quantitative image analysis of FSC clone sizes in mosaic ovarioles showed average clone sizes of approximately 50% (50.1±14.1% at 7dphs, 51.3±18.0% at 14dphs with four heat shocks; 48.2±14.8% with single heat shock; 44.7±10.4% with MARCM), consistent across different induction protocols and marking systems, supporting two active FSCs per ovariole but consistent with fluctuation between one to four FSCs.
evaluation: Claims C97-C106 present rigorous quantitative analysis with multiple independent approaches (different heat shock regimens, different clonal systems), appropriate statistical comparisons (p>0.5), and sufficient sample sizes. The methodology is clearly described in Figure 4A-B, and the conclusion appropriately acknowledges variability (±14-18%) while supporting the two FSC model.

result: Analysis of FSC position relative to FasIII expression showed that in 85.7% of ovarioles with FSC clones, the anterior-most GFP negative cell was FasIII positive at the FasIII expression boundary, with remaining cases likely representing FSCs with low FasIII expression (7.9%) or IGS cell labeling (6.3%), confirming FSCs are usually FasIII positive and reside at the FasIII expression boundary.
evaluation: Claims C107-C117 provide quantitative positional analysis (n=63) with clear categorization and appropriate interpretation of ambiguous cases. The data are consistent with prior literature (C111) and include appropriate controls (C116). Alternative explanations for minority cases are appropriately considered. Data shown in Figure 5A-E.

result: The two FSC model is consistent with published rates of oogenesis and follicle cell number: two FSCs dividing with 9.6 hour cell cycle would take ~85 hours to produce 900 cells (transit time ~100 hours), while 16 FSCs would take only 56 hours. Multiple independent lines of evidence from prior studies support a small number of FSCs and are inconsistent with 15-16 FSCs spanning Region 2a and 2b.
evaluation: Claims C118-C127 provide mathematical validation of the two FSC model using published parameters with correct calculations and appropriate biological reasoning. The argument is strengthened by citing multiple independent lines of evidence from prior literature. The mathematical logic is sound and dimensional analysis is correct.

result: The LGR system's unreliability stems from high background clone induction and unexpected marker combinations, possibly due to non-canonical recombination events or epigenetic silencing of marker transgenes. High fluorophore expression may create selective pressure for silencing, and epigenetic silencing of transgenes has been previously documented in follicle cells.
evaluation: Claims C128-C138 appropriately summarize problems with the LGR system but the mechanistic explanations (C129-C136) are speculative. While epigenetic silencing is documented in follicle cells (C134), the cited study used UAS promoters rather than constitutive promoters (C135), limiting direct applicability. The speculation is reasonable but unproven.

result: The neutral drift analysis in Reilein et al. is flawed because it does not explain why clonal diversity would decline to two lineages and remain stable rather than continuing to monoclonality. The observed clonal diversity at early timepoints is better explained by transient clones that had not yet moved out of the tissue rather than neutral drift among many FSCs.
evaluation: Claims C139-C148 provide valid logical critique of the Reilein et al. analysis. The observation that neutral drift models predict monoclonality not biclonality (C142) is correct. The alternative explanation (C147) is more parsimonious given the data on clone contiguity (C143-C144) and is supported by the authors' own observations.

result: The approach in Reilein et al. of measuring the fraction of a follicle labeled by rare FSC clones is invalid within their own framework because they propose different proliferation rates among FSCs, which would cause more rapidly dividing FSCs to be preferentially labeled and contribute disproportionately to the tissue, skewing stem cell number estimates by an unknown amount.
evaluation: Claims C149-C155 identify an internal logical inconsistency in the Reilein et al. study. The reasoning is sound: if FSCs have different proliferation rates (C151) and mitosis is required for labeling (C152), then the assumption of equal labeling probability (C150) is violated. The conclusion (C155) follows logically.

result: The assumption that FRT recombination occurs in 100% of mitotic cells predicts that every ovariole should have all six marker phenotypes at early timepoints (5 dphs) given thousands of mitotic follicle cells per ovariole, but this was not observed in either the current study or Reilein et al., suggesting the neutral drift analysis overestimated initial clonal diversity and FSC number.
evaluation: Claims C156-C160 present a logical reductio ad absurdum argument. The prediction (C158) follows logically from the assumption, and the empirical observation (C159) contradicts the prediction. The inference about overestimation (C160) is reasonable though the magnitude of error is uncertain.

result: Despite variability in clone size and pattern, the findings reinforce that two FSCs produce the majority of follicle epithelium in most cases, though the quantitative approach revealed more variability than previously thought, leaving open the possibility that FSC number fluctuates within a range of one to four.
evaluation: Claims C161, C168-C169 appropriately synthesize the clone size data (from C99-C106) acknowledging both the central tendency (two FSCs) and the observed variability. The conclusion is appropriately qualified and consistent with the standard deviations reported in the quantitative analysis.

result: Somatic cells in Region 2a have distinct characteristics from follicle epithelium, making it unlikely that FSCs span this border. Live imaging in Reilein et al. showed cell movement but could not confirm cell identity. Under normal laboratory conditions, persistent FSC clones are typically contained within the FasIII expression domain, though further analysis is needed to determine if cells can convert between IGS and follicle cell identities.
evaluation: Claims C162-C165 provide reasonable interpretation based on established knowledge about cell types (C162), appropriate critique of prior work (C163), and qualified conclusions (C165) based on the positional data from C107-C117. The acknowledgment of future work needed (C164) is appropriate.

result: The study clarifies and reaffirms the current paradigm for fundamental features of the Drosophila FSC lineage and provides important context for studies using the follicle epithelium as a model system.
evaluation: Claims C166-C167 appropriately summarize the overall significance of the work. The study provides multiple independent lines of evidence supporting the two FSC model and identifies specific problems with the Reilein et al. study, justifying these broad conclusions.

result: The Drosophila ovary follicle stem cells are an important and well-established model system for epithelial stem cell biology, with decades of research supporting fundamental organizational principles and diverse insights into epithelial biology including cell fate specification, polarity, and planar polarity mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C8-C13 establish the scientific context through citations to established literature. These are appropriate background claims supported by the cited references and represent established scientific consensus.

result: The Drosophila ovary has a stereotypical organization with ovarioles containing germaria with four distinct regions (1, 2a, 2b, 3), where GSCs in Region 1 produce cystoblasts that develop through Region 2a (covered by IGS cells) into Region 2b where they are encapsulated by follicle cells, then bud off as Stage 2 follicles in a continuous ~8-9 day process.
evaluation: Claims C14-C27 describe established anatomical and developmental features of the Drosophila ovary, supported by citations to foundational literature and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A. This is well-established background knowledge.

result: The Margolis and Spradling study was a landmark work that identified FSCs using site-specific DNA recombination for lineage tracing, establishing principles and quality control measures for clonal analysis that became gold standards applied to many other stem cell lineages in Drosophila and mammals.
evaluation: Claims C28-C36 accurately describe the historical significance and methodological contributions of the Margolis and Spradling study, supported by appropriate citations. These establish important context for evaluating subsequent work.

result: Margolis and Spradling observed that single FSC clones contribute to an average of 50% of follicle cells on Stage 10 follicles, remain coherent as contiguous patches, and always include cells at the Region 2a/2b border, leading to their conclusion of two actively dividing FSCs per ovariole residing at the Region 2a/2b border.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 accurately summarize key findings from the Margolis and Spradling study that are being re-evaluated in the current work. These are appropriate citations to prior work.

result: Reilein et al. concluded there are 15-16 actively dividing FSCs per germarium organized in three rings, with individual FSC clones potentially discontinuous, based primarily on a novel LGR clonal marking system using three markers and two pairs of FRT sites that can produce six marker combinations.
evaluation: Claims C41-C45 accurately describe the findings and methods from Reilein et al. that are being challenged in the current study. The description of the LGR system is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

result: The authors identified several problems with the Reilein et al. study, developed new quantitative methods for measuring clone size, found that FSC clones produce on average half the follicle cells per ovariole, and conclude there are typically two active FSCs per ovariole though consistent with up to four FSCs per germarium.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 accurately summarize the main findings of the current study, which are supported by the detailed results presented in the manuscript. These serve as appropriate abstract-level summaries of the work.

result: Reilein et al. reported that anterior-most cells labeled with the LGR system were located within three adjacent positions leading up to the FasIII border and interpreted this as evidence for FSCs in three rings including two FasIII negative rings in Region 2a.
evaluation: Claim C108 accurately describes findings and interpretation from the Reilein et al. study that are being challenged by the current positional analysis. This is appropriate citation to prior work.
